11.	The Latin verb ________ means “to pull apart, divide, set aside.” From this verb, English borrowed three words at different times, and all three are still in everyday use. The first borrowing X came in the 12th century via Old French. It still means just what the Latin meant: to cut apart or divide, used in surgery, in business (e.g. when parting ways with an employee), and in legal compensation contexts. The second borrowing Y came in the 15th century directly from Latin, retaining both the sound and the meaning. Y is most common English descendant — to put apart, or as an adjective, distinct. The third borrowing Z came also in the 15th century, via Anglo-French. It originally meant “each one Y-ly distinct” — emphasizing that members of a group should be considered individually rather than collectively. From there it drifted to mean “more than two but not many,” which is the modern sense. The original meaning survives today in just one place: the legal phrase “joint and Z liability.” ID X (5 points), Y (5 points), and Z (5 points).

12.	The Latin verb ______ means “to do” or “to make,” and its past participle, ______, means “a thing done” or “a thing made.” English borrowed this past participle three times, and the three resulting words are all so common that you may not notice their shared root. The first borrowing X came in the 14th century via Old French. It originally meant simply “an act” or “a deed,” but narrowed in English to mean an impressive act — usually one requiring skill, strength, or daring. The second borrowing Y came directly from Latin in the 16th century. It originally meant “an act done,” but in English it drifted away from the act itself toward the idea of something that has demonstrably occurred — and from there to “something that is the case, something verifiably true.” The third borrowing Z came via Old French, originally meaning “the way something is made, its form.” In English it was first applied to the form of the human face, then generalized to any prominent characteristic of anything. Z is used today, among other things, to list the capabilities of any software product. ID X (5 points), Y (5 points), and Z (5 points).
